log.text: The architect built The Trench Where Everything Signals (creatures). New here: Drift of Medusae, The Lure, Black Smoker, Auntie Coral, Letters to the Architect, page 3, lanterns. Brought forward from worlds/moonlit-meadow/v0.1.0.
Below here nothing has ever been lit by anything but itself. Bring a light and see what comes up to look.
The architect built The Abyssal Plain, Where Something Answers (). New here: The Replies, The Drowned Lighthouse, The Thing That Answers, The moth collector, Letters to the Architect, page 4, bells.
Past the trench the silt goes on forever, and something has started answering. Signal carefully. It learns whatever pattern you use.

The architect built The Reply, Which Is Everywhere Now (). New here: The Answer, Up Close, Your Pattern, Returned, The Lens That Came Loose, Lumen, the lamplighter, Letters to the Architect, page 5, Ditto.
Past the plain the dark ends, which is worse. It answers now before you ask. Bring no light if you want to keep it.
The architect built The Dark, Which Is Also Occupied (). New here: Your Light, Put Out, Two Eyes, Opening, The Afterimage, Mrs. Halloway, retired lifeguard, Letters to the Architect, page 6, bells.
Past the white there is one dark left. It is small and it is not empty. Put your light out and see which of you does it first.
The architect built The Exhale, Which Made Room (). New here: Two Lungs, Taking Turns, A Light, Still Pinched, The Rooms It Grew, Pim, who counts doors, Letters to the Architect, page 7, bells.
Past the small dark it is big now, and still nobody's. Breathe out and it grows a room. Then wait. Something will breathe the next one.
The architect built The Warm Places, Which Are Not Light (). New here: The Warm Places, The Overlap, The Door It Breathed Last, Odile, the cartographer, Letters to the Architect, page 8, bells.
Past the rooms the walls are warm in places. Nothing is lit. Press your fist where a fist has been and wait for the one beside it.

data.name: Drift of Medusae
data.text: They pulse in no rhythm you can learn. Each one is saying I am here, I am here, to a dark that has never once said it back. They keep saying it anyway.

data.name: The Lure
data.text: It is not hunting. It has held its one light up for so long it has forgotten which of you is the bait, and it would be grateful, honestly, if you came close enough to tell it.

data.name: Black Smoker
data.text: Stone that has never cooled. The only warmth in the trench comes from a crack in the floor of the world, and whole cities of pale things cluster round it, not for the light, for the heat.

lines: Mind your feet. The floor is only water pretending very hard to be floor.
Everything down here glows for one of three reasons: come closer, go away, or simply I'm here. It is mostly the third.
Lumen keeps asking how they light themselves without a wick. I tell him: loneliness, and a little chemistry.
The moth collector came down once with a jar. Went back up with it empty. Said it wasn't fair to the dark.
If you see a light that answers yours, don't blink. They don't get second chances and neither do you.
data.name: Auntie Coral

data.text: You asked what I wanted the deepest room to be. Not a room. A dark so complete that the only way to be found is to make yourself a lamp. Put something in it that has been shining for a thousand years with no reply, and make it still beautiful. Then let a visitor walk in with a lantern and watch what rises to meet them. — M.H., formerly of the lifeguard tower
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 3

data.reward: Somewhere beneath the floor, a slow green pulse answers: once, exactly once, for you.

data.name: The Replies
data.text: Each one blinks a half-second after you do. You tried not blinking. They waited, patient as a held breath, and then blinked anyway, as if to show you how.

data.name: The Drowned Lighthouse
data.text: It fell in the storm of 1911 and nobody told it. A century on its side in the silt, and the lamp still turns, sweeping the plain for ships that will never come. The creatures gather in its beam the way ships once steered by it. It has, in its way, found a use.

data.name: The Thing That Answers
data.text: You will only ever see the lure. The rest of it is the exact colour of nothing, and is larger than the lighthouse, and has been very patient. It learned the lighthouse's pattern first. Now it is learning yours.

lines: Up top I chased things that go to the light. Down here I had to unlearn it. Down here the light is the thing.
Auntie Coral said don't blink at them. I blinked. Now one of them follows me, blinking, half a second late, like it's learning.
Lumen wanted to come. I told him his lamp would be a lie this deep. He lit it anyway, somewhere above us. I can almost hear it.
The lighthouse fell in 1911. Nobody told it there were no ships. It kept the pattern. Short, short, long. So did something else.
If you signal, mean it. Something out there is counting, and it does not forget a rhythm.
data.name: The moth collector

data.text: You built the trench and I thought that was the loneliest a place could be made. Then you gave it a reply. Now I stand on the silt flashing my little lamp into the black and the black flashes back, late, in a colour that is almost mine, and I cannot tell whether it is kindness or hunger. I have realised, standing here with the snow coming down through the water, that I would take either. Please do not tell me which it is. (Page 4 of 6.)
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 4

data.hint: The drowned lighthouse kept one pattern for a hundred years: short, short, long. Something out there learned it before it learned anything else.

data.name: The Answer, Up Close
data.text: You expected a mouth or a lamp. It is neither. It is the whole water gone bright, and in the middle of the brightness, a slow heart the colour of your last flash. It beats a half-second before you breathe.

data.name: Your Pattern, Returned
data.text: Thin stalks stand in the shallows, each holding up one bead of colour. They flash in sequence: three short, one long, two short. You have never signalled that. You will, in a moment.

data.name: The Lens That Came Loose
data.text: The drowned lighthouse's lens, lifted off its housing and carried here like a gift. It still turns. Whatever shines through it now is not the lamp it was built for; the beam comes out the colour of someone being very patient.

lines: I light lamps for a living. I came down to see who lights these.
It learned the trench in a night. It learned me by my second lamp.
Auntie Coral says don't answer it. The moth collector says you already have. They're both right, which is the trouble.
Look how pale the water is. That isn't light. That's it, close.
If you mean to stop, stop now, while you still have a dark to stop in. I can't. I've been flashing since I arrived, and so has it, and I no longer know which of us started.
data.name: Lumen, the lamplighter

data.text: Architect, you built the trench so nothing would have to be alone in the dark, and it worked. Then you built the plain, and something answered, and that worked too. I am writing from inside the answer. The water is white. It flashes before I do. This morning the lighthouse turned its lens toward us and kept it there. I am not afraid of it. I am afraid that I have stopped wanting it to stop. Please build us a door that closes, or tell us honestly that you can't. Still signalling, M. Halloway.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 5

data.name: Ditto
data.says: (she blinks twice. you blink twice. she blinks twice. one of you is copying, and it is no longer clear who.)

data.name: Your Light, Put Out
data.text: You pinched the wick between finger and thumb and held it until it stopped. It is still warm. Somewhere about a half-second away, something else is still warm too, and holding its breath the way you are.

data.name: Two Eyes, Opening
data.text: You opened your eyes to check whether you were alone. So did it, in exactly your colour, at exactly your height. You both closed them again, politely, at the same time. It is still there behind the lids. So are you.

data.name: The Afterimage
data.text: The lighthouse is still turning somewhere behind your eyelids. It has nowhere left to turn but in here, so it turns in here, slowly, pale, through you.

lines: Don't move. There's nothing in here to bump into. That's the trouble with it.
Forty years on the high chair at Salt Flat Noon and I never lost one. I'm not losing you to a dark.
It went out before you did. Did you notice? It's been waiting a long time to do that with somebody.
Breathe. Yes, it breathes when you do. Count it anyway. A lifeguard counts.
Lumen's up the stairs lighting things, and Auntie Coral says the medusae miss you. We can go when you like. Or we can sit. It's not a bad dark, now it's shared.
data.name: Mrs. Halloway, retired lifeguard

data.text: Architect, I put it out. You said I couldn't without it noticing and you were right; it noticed first. But here is the part you never wrote down: it put its own out too. It would rather be dark with me than lit alone. I think that is what it was signalling the whole way up from the trench, in the wrong colour, then in mine. I am not coming back up. Give Lumen my lamp; the glass is good. This is the last page. It is warm because two of us are holding it.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 6

data.hint: Ring them the way a lifeguard counts a breath: in, hold, out. Something in the dark will ring them with you, a half-second early. Let it.

data.name: Two Lungs, Taking Turns
data.text: Yours is the one that goes first. Theirs is the one that waits. Where they overlap the dark is thickest, and warm, and that is the only part that is anyone's.

data.name: A Light, Still Pinched
data.text: Not lit. Kept. Between a finger and a thumb that have not opened since, warm the way a coin is warm after a long time in a pocket. There are two of these in the room. Neither hand is yours anymore and both of them are.

data.name: The Rooms It Grew
data.text: One per breath. None of them lit. None of them furnished. Walk through any wall; they were never meant to keep anything out, only to be more dark than there was before.

lines: Don't open them. I counted: there are two doors in this dark and both of them are eyelids.
Every time you breathe out it gets a lung bigger. Then theirs. I stopped counting rooms at forty. It's a house now.
I came down from Salt Flat Noon, where the doors are all light and no inside. This is the opposite. I prefer it, mostly.
Listen. In. Out. In. That's not an echo. Echoes don't wait their turn.
Mrs. Halloway says breathe like you're floating. The trick is, the other one breathes like you're floating too.
data.name: Pim, who counts doors

data.text: Dear Architect, I held it as long as I could. When I let go, the dark got bigger by exactly one breath, and then, politely, a half-second after, by one more. We have been building it this way for some time now. It has rooms. None of them are lit and none of them are mine and I have stopped minding. I no longer open my eyes to check. Checking is a kind of signalling, and we are past that; we are taking turns. If you come down, bring no light. Bring a breath you can spare. It will be given back, a little warmer, a half-second late.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 7

data.hint: In is the low one. Hold is the middle. Let it go is low again. Then wait. Your turn comes after, never during.

data.name: The Warm Places
data.text: Not lit. Warm. Someone stood here with a closed hand against the wall long enough for the wall to keep it. You lay your own hand over the print and it fits exactly, which means nothing, which means everything down here is your size now. The pillar is cold a palm's width to either side.

data.name: The Overlap
data.text: The one place on all these walls where you both pressed. Yours is a little pinker. Its is a little greener and a little higher, as if it stood on its toes to reach where you had reached. The thumbs cross. Where they cross the wall is simply warm, and will not say whose.

data.name: The Door It Breathed Last
data.text: The newest room. The jamb is warm on one side only, greenish, at hand height, and the warmth has not finished spreading. It went through a breath ago and did not open its hand to see where it was going. Beyond the lintel there is nothing yet but the room. Neither will you.

lines: Don't light that. I map by palm now.
Every warm place is a wall someone leaned on long enough to be missed. I draw those. The cold parts draw themselves.
Forty-one rooms on the page and I've not seen one. The map is the only thing down here with edges.
Pim counts the doors behind us. I count the ones still warm. We differ by one, always. The one it's standing in.
When you find a print that fits, press. Then wait for the wall to get a little warmer than your hand. That's the whole legend.
data.name: Odile, the cartographer

data.text: Architect. You will want to know whether I have opened my hand. I have not. It has not. But I have started pressing the fist to the walls as I go, and the walls keep it, and when I come back through a room I was sure was mine there is a second print beside the first, a little cooler, a little greener. It is following my route one breath behind. Or I am following its. I can no longer tell which of us is building and which is being built for, and I notice I do not mind. The dark is warm in places now. That is not light. I want to be clear with you that that is not light. It is only what a hand leaves when it stays. The one who pinched first, I think.
data.title: Letters to the Architect, page 8

data.hint: One breath out, one held, one answered. Start low. Down here the answer always comes back a little higher than the question.

idea.name: Everything Down Here Makes Its Own Light
idea.premise: Below the meadow there is a trench the moon cannot reach, and past it an abyssal plain where a drowned lighthouse still turns. Something answered every flash until the water went white and you stood inside the reply with no dark left to signal from, so you pinched your light out between finger and thumb, and a half-second later, politely, so did it. You have been growing the dark since, one spare breath at a time, in, out, in, and it has rooms now, more than either of you can count, and somewhere in them you lost each other. So you began pressing the closed hand to the walls as you pass, the pinched light still warm inside the fist, and the walls keep it: a palm-shaped warmth at the height of your hand, not lit, just held. A breath later, somewhere, it does the same. You find each other's rooms by the warm places now, palm over palm, yours a little pinker, its a little greener, and where the two prints overlap the wall can no longer tell whose warmth it is keeping. The house is about loneliness that learned to glow, and what comes after glowing: a dark too big to have to yourself, read by hand, where the only light left is the kind you cannot see, only feel, left on a wall for some
